en: The Jātaka:
The Section of Thirty, Chapter on Kiṁchanda.
8. The Paṇḍara Nāga King Jātaka:
"One who speaks incoherently, who does not conceal his counsel, who is unrestrained, and who does not look ahead;”
Fear follows that one who lacks understanding,
just as the supaṇṇa bird pursues a pale white elephant;
this applies to whoever would guard a secret counsel.
A person deluded by ignorance speaks with laughter;
that broken counsel quickly brings danger upon him,
just as the supaṇṇa bird devours a white elephant.
One who is merely a nominal friend is not fit to understand a secret matter of weight;
nor is even a true friend fit to understand that which has not been realized.
Or [I spoke] what was meaningless to the Fully Awakened One.
I placed my trust in the naked ascetic, thinking,
"This one is considered a true ascetic, one who has developed his self."
I revealed to her that secret meaning;
though the matter was past, I weep for the wretched one.
O Brahmā, I [reveal] that supreme secret to her.
For I was unable to restrain my speech;
because of that, fear has come upon me, and now,
with my purpose past, I weep like a wretch.
That man who, thinking he is a friend,
reveals a secret matter to one of low birth— whether out of malice,
fear, or passion— [is a fool].
The fool who, when among assemblies,
utters words that cause delight— his speech being out of harmony— he is undoubtedly one who has entered into the company of the wicked.
They call such a man a venomous snake with a foul face;
one should stay far, very far away from such a person.
[One should avoid] food, drink, Kāsī cloth, and sandalwood [from him].
“Leaving behind our beloved backsides and our garlands and ointments,
we go, abandoning all sensual pleasures;
O Supaṇṇa, we have indeed become like living beings.”
“Who here, O King of Nagas, among the living beings in this world, incurs reproach when three have crossed over?
Is it the ascetic, the Supanna, or indeed you yourself?”
“For what reason was he taken by Paṇḍaraka?
“Because he was considered by me to be a true ascetic,
and because that self-realized one was dear to my mind.”
I have revealed to her the hidden meaning;
having understood the past, I weep for my wretchedness.
"There is no being on earth that is immortal."
There is no kind of wisdom that should not be praised;
by means of truth, the Dhamma, fortitude, and self-control,
a person here speaks only what is unattainable [by others].
Parents are the supreme among kinsmen;
there is no third who is so compassionate.
One should not disclose their secret to others.
Fearing the disclosure of his secret counsel,
even those who are his mother, father, sisters, brothers,
or companions who stand on his side—
One should not disclose even their supreme secret,
fearing the disclosure of counsel;
even if a wife should speak against her husband, one should remain silent.
The maiden was pleasant-spoken,
endowed with a son, beauty, and fame,
and surrounded by a host of kinsmen.
One should not disclose even her most secret [thought],
fearing the betrayal of counsel;
one should not reveal a secret matter.
One should guard it as if it were a treasure; for a wise person,
a secret matter is better kept hidden than revealed.
A wise person should not disclose a secret to a woman or to an enemy,
nor to one who can be bribed with material gain.
And the man who is a thief of the heart:
that man who awakens another person to a secret matter they have not yet understood.
Out of fear of the loss of his status as a minister,
he remains patient like a servant;
for as long as there is any purpose for a man—
The wise know a secret; as many [as there are who know it], so many are his anxieties.
Therefore, one should not disclose a secret.
One should speak in private during the day;
at night, one should not let loose speech beyond measure;
for eavesdroppers listen for secret counsel.
Therefore, the spell quickly meets with failure.
Just as if there were a great city,
made of iron, with auspicious walls, yet lacking gates;
Surrounded by moats and trenches—
such are these secret mantras of mine here.
These secret mantras belong to those who do not scatter their speech.
Firm in their own welfare are those men who have tongues difficult to guard;
from them enemies keep far away,
as if from a swarm of venomous snakes.
“Having abandoned the home life, gone forth as a naked ascetic,
shaven-headed and without clothing, he wanders for the sake of food;
in him indeed have I revealed the hidden meaning.”
Wealth and Dhamma have been lost to us.
O King of Supaṇṇas, how should one act?
What is his character, and by what conduct should he live?
“How does a recluse, wandering about and having abandoned all things cherished,
attain the heavenly state?
“By being endowed with moral shame, patience, and self-control,” [he replied].
Free from anger, having abandoned slander,
and practicing as a recluse while relinquishing all things held as "mine"— acting thus, one goes to the heavenly realm.
“Just as a mother’s touch spreads through her tender,
delicate infant’s entire body,
so too have you appeared before me, O Lord of Birds.”
“O double-tongued one, release him today from execution out of compassion for your son;
for he is my third son, and indeed there is no other.”
"A resident pupil, one given [as a gift], and one born of my own body— each was a son of mine in turn.
Thus did the Supaṇṇa respond with these words.
Having established himself upon the earth, the twice-born [Garuda] said to the double-tongued one:
"You have now become free from all fear; whether on land or in water, you shall be protected by me."
As a skilled physician is to those who are ill,
as a cool lake is to those who are thirsty,
as a dwelling is to those tormented by the cold of snow;
“Even so do I become your refuge.
“Having made an alliance with an enemy—
whether born from an egg or born from a womb,”
“Having bared his fangs he lies there;
from where has this fear come upon you?
“I am indeed suspicious of my enemy.”
One should not place trust even in a friend;
from fearlessness, fear arises,
even cutting down one's very roots.
How indeed can one trust him with whom a quarrel has been made?
One must stand firm in constant self-restraint.
He is not attached to forms.
He should inspire confidence in others but not place his own trust in them;
he should be suspicious where there is no cause for suspicion.
In such a way should the wise man exert himself, so that others may not know his true state.
Those beings of divine appearance and delicate form—
Both masses of merit, equally well-conquered,
approached the naked ascetic Karambiya,
like two well-trained elephants mingling their ichor.
Then Paṇḍaraka, having approached the naked ascetic himself,
said this: “I am liberated,
having abandoned all things and transcended all fear.”
"Surely he was not dear to your mind?
"The king of the supaṇṇas was indeed dear to me;
there is no doubt that this is true because of Paṇḍaraka."
Thus, being impassioned by lust,
I committed this evil deed with full awareness, not out of delusion.
"Neither what is dear nor what is not dear to me exists," [he said].
Having clearly perceived this world and the next,
you wander through this world unrestrained, like one who speaks with the voice of those who are well-restrained.
Whether you are noble or ignoble,
unrestrained yet appearing restrained,
dark by birth and ignoble in form—
You have committed much evil and misconduct.
You were treacherous toward one who was not hostile,
and you are both treacherous and slanderous.
“By this utterance of truth,
may your head split into seven pieces!
“Therefore, one should never betray friends.”
There is no other more wicked than one who betrays a friend;
with his heart inflamed by passion, he was struck down upon the earth,
for Saṃvara was slain at the word of Indra.
The Paṇḍara Nāga King Jātaka, the eighth.
